title: Contract-to-Close: Contingency Management, Timelines & Escrow Coordination
body_markdown:
## Learning Objectives

By the end of this unit you will be able to:

1. **Build** a transaction timeline from the acceptance date and calendar every deadline.
2. **Manage** contingency removal under California's active removal regime.
3. **Apply** the notice to perform and cancellation procedures correctly.
4. **Coordinate** escrow, lender, title, and inspection workflows.
5. **Negotiate** repair requests without converting an as-is sale into a warranty.
6. **Diagnose** the common causes of failed escrows and intervene early.
7. **Calculate** deadline dates and understand what "time is of the essence" makes material.

---

## 1. Day One: Build the Timeline

The single highest-value hour in any transaction is the one immediately after acceptance, spent building the calendar.

**From the acceptance date, calendar:**

| Item | Typical timing |
|---|---|
| Deposit into escrow | Within 3 business days of acceptance |
| Escrow opened, instructions out | Days 1–3 |
| Seller disclosures delivered | Immediately (ideally pre-offer) |
| Preliminary report ordered and delivered | Days 1–7 |
| Inspections scheduled | Days 1–5 |
| Investigation contingency | Commonly 17 days |
| Appraisal and loan contingencies | Commonly 21 days |
| Loan documents to escrow | Days 21–28 |
| Final walk-through | Days before closing |
| Signing, funding, recording | Final days |

Those contingency periods are **contractual, not statutory** — read the actual contract every time. <!-- VERIFY: current standard-form default periods -->

**Counting convention:** day one is generally the day *after* acceptance. Confirm against the form you are using, and when a deadline is ambiguous, resolve it in writing with the other agent rather than assuming.

**Because "time is of the essence" applies, every one of those dates is material.** A missed date is a breach, not a delay.

## 2. Contingency Removal: Active, Not Automatic

California residential practice uses **active removal** (Principles Unit 8). This is the single most misunderstood mechanic in the transaction, and getting it wrong costs deals.

**What it means:**

- Contingencies remain in effect **until the buyer removes them in writing**.
- A deadline passing does **not** automatically remove a contingency and does **not** automatically permit the seller to cancel.
- When a deadline passes without removal, the seller's remedy is to deliver a **Notice to Buyer to Perform**, which starts a cure period. Only after that period runs may the seller cancel.

**Notice to Perform mechanics:**
- Must be in writing and properly delivered.
- Gives the buyer a stated period to act — commonly two days, but read the form. <!-- VERIFY: current notice period on the standard form -->
- May generally not be delivered earlier than a stated number of days before the underlying deadline.

**The two failure modes:**

1. **The seller's agent who cancels on the deadline.** No notice, no cure period, unilateral cancellation. This is a wrongful cancellation and the seller may be in breach.
2. **The buyer's agent who assumes a passed deadline is harmless.** It is not — it hands the seller the right to start the notice clock and creates leverage the buyer did not intend to give.

**Cancellation requires mutual written instructions** to release the deposit (Principles Unit 10). Escrow does not decide who is right. When both sides claim the deposit, escrow holds it until they agree or a court orders release — which is why "you'll get your deposit back" is a sentence you should never say casually.

## 3. Inspections and Repair Requests

**Schedule inspections immediately.** The investigation period is short and inspectors book out. A buyer's agent who schedules on day 12 of a 17-day period has created an avoidable crisis.

**Common inspections:** general home inspection, termite/wood-destroying organism, roof, sewer lateral (increasingly essential on older properties), chimney, pool/spa, foundation or structural where indicated, and specialized environmental where the property suggests it.

**The repair request conversation.** After inspections, buyers typically ask for repairs or credits. Practical guidance:

- **Prioritize by materiality**, not by item count. Health and safety, structural, systems, and anything affecting insurability or financing come first. A list of 40 cosmetic items reads as unserious and hardens the seller.
- **Credits often work better than repairs.** The seller avoids managing contractors, and the buyer controls the quality of the work. Note that lenders limit how much credit may be applied. <!-- VERIFY: current seller-credit limits by loan type -->
- **"As-is" does not mean no negotiation.** It means the seller has not agreed in advance to repair. The buyer may still request, and the seller may still say no — and the buyer may still cancel within their contingency (Principles Unit 9).
- **Do not turn the seller into a warrantor.** Careless language in a repair addendum can create ongoing obligations after closing. Keep it specific: what will be done, by whom, by when, and with what evidence of completion.

**Disclosure obligation runs both ways.** If a buyer's inspection reveals a material defect and the transaction later falls through, the **seller now knows** about it and must disclose it to subsequent buyers. Sellers are frequently surprised by this. Tell them before inspections, not after.

## 4. Coordinating the Parties

You are, functionally, the project manager.

**Escrow** needs: the fully executed contract and all addenda, the deposit, the parties' contact and vesting information, payoff demands, and the parties' signed instructions. Escrow acts only on **mutual written instructions** and cannot advise either party (Principles Unit 10).

**The lender** needs: the contract, appraisal access, and the buyer's documents — and needs them promptly. The most common cause of a delayed closing is a buyer who takes nine days to send a bank statement.

**Title** needs: the preliminary report reviewed and any curative items started early. A name-variance judgment lien takes days to clear if you start on day 3 and kills the closing if you start on day 25.

**Weekly communication** is the standard your clients actually judge you on. Even "nothing changed this week, here's where we are" prevents the anxious call.

## 5. Why Escrows Fail — and Early Warning Signs

| Cause | Early warning | Intervention |
|---|---|---|
| Loan denial | Buyer slow on documents; changed jobs; new debt | Verify underwriting status weekly; tell buyers not to open credit or change jobs |
| Low appraisal | Aggressive price with thin comparables | Prepare the seller at the offer stage; assemble comps for the appraiser (facts only) |
| Inspection shock | No pre-offer walkthrough; older property | Set condition expectations early; schedule inspections day one |
| Title defect | Prelim not read; name variance; unreleased lien | Read the prelim day one; start curative work immediately |
| Insurance unavailable | Property in a fire hazard severity zone | Have buyers quote insurance in the first days, not the last |
| Buyer's home not selling | Contingent offer | Monitor the dependent transaction weekly |
| Cold feet | Communication goes quiet | Call, do not text; find out what changed |

**The pattern:** almost every escrow that dies gave a signal a week or more before. Agents who check in weekly catch them; agents who go quiet until the closing date do not.

## 6. Worked Examples

### Example 1 — Building the calendar (Rancho Cucamonga)

Offer accepted **Tuesday, September 8**. Investigation 17 days, loan and appraisal 21 days, close of escrow 30 days.

**Walkthrough** (day one = the day after acceptance, September 9):
1. Deposit to escrow: within **3 business days** → by **Friday, September 11**
2. Investigation contingency: September 9 + 16 = **Friday, September 25**
3. Loan and appraisal: September 9 + 20 = **Tuesday, September 29**
4. Close of escrow: September 9 + 29 = **Thursday, October 8**
5. Final walk-through: schedule **October 5–7**

**Backward-planning from those dates:**
- Inspections must be **completed and reviewed** by ~September 22 to leave room to negotiate repairs before the 25th.
- So inspections get scheduled **September 9–11**, not the week of the 21st.
- The appraisal must be ordered immediately to return before the 29th.

That backward pass is the actual work. The deadline dates are arithmetic; the schedule that makes them achievable is judgment.

### Example 2 — The deadline passed. Now what? (Ontario)

It is September 26. The buyer has not delivered a written investigation contingency removal. The listing agent tells the seller they can cancel and take the backup offer.

**Analysis.** The listing agent is **wrong**, and acting on that advice would put the seller in breach.

Under active removal:
1. The contingency **remains in effect** — it did not expire on its own.
2. The seller may deliver a **Notice to Buyer to Perform**, which starts a short cure period.
3. Only if the buyer fails to remove within that period may the seller cancel.
4. Cancellation then requires **mutual written instructions** to release the deposit.

**What the buyer's agent should do the moment the deadline passes:** contact the listing agent, explain the status, and either deliver the removal or request a written extension. Silence is what turns an administrative slip into a cancellation.

### Example 3 — The repair request that hardened the seller (Covina)

Inspection reveals: a failing water heater (~$1,800), an active roof leak (~$4,500), a cracked heat exchanger in the furnace (safety, ~$5,200), and 31 cosmetic items including loose outlet covers and a sticking closet door. The buyer's agent submits all 34 items.

**Analysis.** The three material items total **$11,500** and are genuinely negotiable — one is a safety issue and two affect systems. Burying them in 34 items invites the seller to reject the whole list as unreasonable, and that is usually what happens.

**Better approach:** request the three material items — ideally as a **credit** of roughly $11,500 rather than repairs, so the buyer controls contractor quality — and explicitly waive the cosmetic list in writing. The waiver is itself a negotiating asset: it signals seriousness and makes the remaining request hard to dismiss.

### Example 4 — The disclosure that follows a failed escrow (Whittier)

A buyer's inspection reveals a cracked sewer lateral. The buyer cancels within their investigation contingency. The seller relists.

**Analysis.** The seller now has **actual knowledge** of a material defect and **must disclose it** to every subsequent buyer (Principles Unit 9). The inspection report does not vanish with the buyer.

Sellers routinely believe a cancelled escrow resets everything. It does not. The professional move is to tell the seller this **before** inspections happen, so they can decide whether to repair proactively — and so they are not blindsided by a disclosure obligation they did not anticipate.

## 7. Key Terms

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Active removal** | The regime under which contingencies remain until removed in writing; deadlines passing do not remove them automatically. |
| **Notice to Buyer to Perform** | The written notice a seller delivers when a buyer misses a deadline, starting a cure period before cancellation is permitted. |
| **Notice to Seller to Perform** | The buyer's corresponding notice when the seller fails to perform a contractual obligation. |
| **Mutual cancellation instructions** | The written agreement of both parties required for escrow to release a deposit. |
| **Time is of the essence** | The clause making each stated deadline material, so late performance is a breach. |
| **Repair request / request for repairs** | The buyer's post-inspection request for repairs or credits; not a right to renegotiate at will. |
| **Seller credit** | Money credited at closing in lieu of repairs; subject to lender limits. |
| **Sewer lateral inspection** | Inspection of the line from the house to the main; increasingly essential on older California properties. |
| **Final walk-through** | The buyer's pre-closing verification of condition and agreed repairs; not a renegotiation opportunity. |

## 8. Practice Tips

- **Build the calendar the day of acceptance**, then plan backward so deadlines are achievable rather than merely known.
- **Schedule inspections in the first three days.** Inspectors book out; the period is short.
- **A passed deadline does not cancel anything.** Deliver a Notice to Perform, run the cure period, then cancel — in that order.
- **Never tell a client their deposit is automatically refundable.** Release requires mutual written instructions.
- **Request the material items, waive the cosmetic ones in writing.** A focused request is a stronger request.
- **Warn sellers before inspections** that discovered defects must be disclosed to future buyers if the escrow fails.
- **Read the preliminary report on day one** and start curative work immediately.
- **Communicate weekly even when nothing has changed.** Silence is how escrows die unnoticed.

## 9. Unit Assessment

The 18-question assessment lives in `/content/question-bank/practice/unit-09.json` with full per-option rationales.

questions.stem: Under California's active removal regime, when a buyer's contingency deadline passes without a written removal:
options: The contingency is automatically removed
The contingency remains in effect and the seller may deliver a Notice to Buyer to Perform
The contract is automatically cancelled
The seller may immediately keep the deposit
rationales: Passive waiver is not the California residential default; contingencies persist until removed in writing.
Correct. The contingency survives the deadline, and the seller's remedy is a written Notice to Buyer to Perform that starts a cure period before cancellation is permitted.
No automatic cancellation occurs, and a seller who cancels on the deadline may be in breach.
Deposit release requires a valid cancellation and mutual written instructions.

questions.stem: A listing agent advises the seller to cancel immediately when the buyer misses the investigation deadline, with no notice delivered. This advice is:
options: Correct, since time is of the essence
Incorrect, and acting on it could place the seller in breach
Correct if a backup offer exists
Correct if the buyer was reminded verbally
rationales: Time is of the essence makes deadlines material but does not eliminate the notice-and-cure procedure.
Correct. Under active removal the seller must deliver a Notice to Buyer to Perform and let the cure period run; unilateral cancellation on the deadline is a wrongful cancellation.
The presence of a backup offer does not change the required procedure.
A verbal reminder is not the written notice the contract requires.

questions.stem: Both parties claim the deposit after a failed transaction. Escrow will:
options: Release it to the party with the stronger claim
Hold it until both parties sign mutual cancellation instructions or a court orders release
Split it evenly
Return it to the buyer automatically
rationales: Escrow does not adjudicate the parties' rights.
Correct. Escrow acts only on mutual written instructions; absent agreement it holds the funds and may interplead them — which is why an agent should never promise a client an automatic refund.
Escrow has no authority to compromise the parties' claims.
Deposits are not automatically refundable.

questions.stem: An offer is accepted Tuesday, September 8, with a 17-day investigation contingency counted from the day after acceptance. Written removal is due no later than:
options: September 24
September 25
September 26
September 29
rationales: September 24 counts only 16 days from September 9.
Correct. Day one is September 9; 17 days runs through September 25 (September 9 plus 16 additional days).
September 26 counts 18 days.
September 29 corresponds to a 21-day contingency such as loan or appraisal.

options: In the final days of the investigation period
Within the first few days after acceptance
After the appraisal is completed
Only if the buyer requests them
rationales: Scheduling late leaves no room to review reports or negotiate repairs before the deadline.
Correct. Inspectors book out and the period is short, so scheduling in the first days leaves time to review findings and negotiate before the contingency expires.
The appraisal is a lender function on a separate track and does not gate inspections.
The agent should recommend inspections proactively rather than waiting to be asked.

questions.stem: A buyer's inspection reveals a cracked sewer lateral and the buyer cancels within their contingency. When the seller relists, the seller:
options: Has no disclosure obligation because that escrow was cancelled
Must disclose the defect to subsequent buyers, because the seller now has actual knowledge
Must disclose only if the next buyer asks
May wait until an offer is accepted to disclose
rationales: Cancellation does not erase the seller's knowledge.
Correct. The seller now has actual knowledge of a material defect and must disclose it to every subsequent buyer — which is why agents should warn sellers of this before inspections occur.
The disclosure duty is affirmative and does not depend on being asked.
Delaying disclosure until after acceptance defeats its purpose and creates a termination right.

questions.stem: Inspections reveal three material items totaling about $11,500 and 31 cosmetic items. The strongest repair request strategy is to:
options: Submit all 34 items so nothing is waived
Request the three material items, ideally as a credit, and waive the cosmetic list in writing
Request only the least expensive item to seem reasonable
Request a price reduction equal to all 34 items
rationales: A 34-item list invites the seller to reject the whole request as unserious, which is usually what happens.

Correct. Focusing on material items — health, safety, structure, and systems — and expressly waiving the cosmetic list signals seriousness and makes the remaining request hard to dismiss. A credit also lets the buyer control contractor quality.
Understating the request forfeits value the buyer is entitled to negotiate.
Valuing cosmetic items into a price reduction produces a number the seller will not accept.

options: Has no obligation to disclose known defects
Has not agreed in advance to make repairs, though the buyer may still request them
May refuse to allow inspections
Is released from all liability after closing
rationales: As-is never waives the duty to disclose known material facts.
Correct. As-is sets repair expectations; the buyer may still request repairs or credits, the seller may decline, and the buyer may still cancel within their contingency.
Buyers retain their investigation rights in an as-is sale.
Liability for concealment or misrepresentation survives closing.

questions.stem: A judgment lien appearing on the preliminary report against someone with the seller's name should be addressed:
options: In the final week before closing
On day one, because curative work takes time
Only if the buyer's lender objects
By ignoring it, since name variances are common
rationales: Waiting until the final week converts a solvable issue into a missed closing.
Correct. Read the preliminary report immediately and start curative work — a name variance resolved by a statement of information takes days if begun early and kills the closing if begun late.
The lender will object, but the agent should not wait for that to act.
Name variances are common and routinely resolved, but only if someone begins the process.

questions.stem: The clause that makes each stated deadline material, so that late performance is a breach rather than a delay, is:
options: The liquidated damages clause
'Time is of the essence'
The active removal provision
The arbitration clause
rationales: Liquidated damages fix an amount payable on breach rather than making deadlines strict.
Correct. 'Time is of the essence' makes every stated date material, which is why the calendar built on the day of acceptance is the highest-value hour in the transaction.
Active removal governs how contingencies are removed, not the materiality of dates.
Arbitration governs dispute resolution.

questions.stem: Escrow may act on instructions that are:
options: Given verbally by either party
Mutual and in writing
Given by the listing agent alone
Implied by the purchase contract
rationales: Verbal instructions are not effective; escrow requires writing.
Correct. As a neutral depository serving both parties, escrow acts only on mutual written instructions and cannot advise or favor either side.
An agent cannot instruct escrow on behalf of both parties.
The contract informs escrow's instructions but does not replace signed mutual instructions.

questions.stem: The most common cause of a delayed closing attributable to the buyer is:
options: Choosing the wrong escrow company
Slow delivery of documents the lender requested
Scheduling the final walk-through late
Requesting a different closing date
rationales: Escrow selection rarely drives timing problems.
Correct. A buyer who takes days to send a bank statement or tax return is the single most common source of delay, which is why agents should monitor underwriting status weekly.
The walk-through occurs near closing and is easily scheduled.
A requested date change is a negotiated term rather than an unplanned delay.

questions.stem: A buyer purchasing a home in a very high fire hazard severity zone should obtain written insurance quotes:
options: After the loan is approved
In the first days of the contingency period
At the final walk-through
After closing
rationales: Loan approval depends in part on insurability, so waiting inverts the sequence.
Correct. Insurance availability and cost in mapped fire zones can prevent closing entirely, so quotes belong at the start of the contingency period rather than the end.
The walk-through is days before closing — far too late to discover a coverage problem.
A buyer who cannot obtain coverage cannot close, so this must be resolved beforehand.

questions.stem: The final walk-through is properly used to:
options: Renegotiate price based on new observations
Verify the property's condition and that agreed repairs were completed
Conduct the buyer's first inspection
Perform the appraisal
rationales: The walk-through is a verification step, not a renegotiation opportunity.
Correct. Its purpose is confirming the property is in the agreed condition and that negotiated repairs were performed.
Inspections belong in the investigation period, not days before closing.
The appraisal is a lender-ordered valuation performed by an appraiser.

questions.stem: A seller credit in lieu of repairs is often preferable to seller-performed repairs because:
options: Credits are unlimited in amount
The buyer controls contractor selection and work quality, and the seller avoids managing the work
Credits do not need to be disclosed to the lender
Credits eliminate the seller's disclosure obligations
rationales: Lenders limit how much credit may be applied, which must be checked before structuring one.
Correct. The buyer chooses the contractor and controls quality while the seller avoids coordinating repairs — usually a better outcome for both.
Credits appear on the settlement statement and are visible to the lender.
Disclosure obligations regarding known defects are unaffected by how repairs are handled.

questions.stem: A buyer's agent realizing a contingency deadline has just passed should:
options: Say nothing and hope the seller does not notice
Contact the listing agent immediately and either deliver the removal or request a written extension
Deliver a Notice to Seller to Perform
Instruct escrow to extend the date
rationales: Silence is what converts an administrative slip into a cancellation.
Correct. Prompt communication with either a written removal or a requested extension resolves the exposure before the seller starts the notice clock.
A Notice to Seller to Perform addresses the seller's failures, not the buyer's.
Escrow cannot amend contract deadlines; only the parties can, in writing.

questions.stem: The most useful early warning that an escrow is failing is typically:
options: A missed closing date
A client who stops responding to communication
The appraisal being ordered
The preliminary report arriving
rationales: By the closing date the failure has already occurred.
Correct. Almost every escrow that dies signals a week or more in advance, and communication going quiet is the most reliable early indicator — call rather than text.
Ordering the appraisal is a routine step.
The preliminary report arriving is expected and routine.

questions.stem: Building the transaction calendar backward from contingency deadlines is valuable primarily because it:
options: Shortens the escrow period
Reveals when inspections and orders must be initiated for the deadlines to be achievable
Eliminates the need for a Notice to Perform
Guarantees the loan will fund on time
rationales: Backward planning does not change the contractual escrow length.
Correct. The deadline dates are arithmetic; determining that inspections must be scheduled in the first three days for a day-25 deadline to be met is the judgment that makes the timeline real.
Notices remain available regardless of planning quality.
No planning guarantees lender performance, though it surfaces problems earlier.
